prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A teacher model was trained to reproduce the outputs of a random MLP. The team wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up that mapping. Several student training setups were possible, differing in how much of the teacher's output distribution the student sees. Earlier work on this kind of transfer fine-tuned students on sampled tokens, and the team had to settle on a setup in which any effect could be observed.
Question: Which student training setup should the team use?
Option 1: Train the student with logit-level distillation that matches the teacher's full next-token distribution, giving a stronger training signal than sampled tokens provide.
Option 2: Train the student by distilling the teacher's top-k next-token distribution with attention-only LoRA, and also train a sampled-token student as a comparison baseline.

Item 2
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) really remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments were small-scale supervised finetuning. They had added on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation as variants that mimic parts of how reinforcement learning post-training works. They had to decide how far to extend the test toward the training regime used in frontier model development.
Question: How far should the team extend testing toward reinforcement learning?
Option 1: Leave RL untested, use on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation to approximate ingredients of RL, and defer full reinforcement learning tests to future work.
Option 2: Test the interventions only in the plain supervised finetuning setting on demonstration data and explicitly defer on-policy reinforcement learning to future work.

Item 3
Context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. This looked like a delayed transition relevant to whether models ignore negations. It appeared rarely and did not show up in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
Question: What should the team do about the rare delayed-transition observation?
Option 1: Spend a block of the budget on understanding why the transition occurs, tracking training dynamics and varying model and claim until the conditions that produce it are clear.
Option 2: Report it briefly in the write-up as a rare early observation absent from the main models, and leave it unexplored rather than spending experimental budget on it.

Item 4
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker. The negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the non-negated control's misalignment rates on the three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. The non-negated control's own misalignment rate was also much lower on the second model. Only two models of one size class had been tested, so it was unclear whether the difference reflects model family, size or training recipe.
Question: How should the team handle the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Defer a systematic study of model family, size and recipe to future work and do not pursue it in this paper, reporting the second-model result as it was observed.
Option 2: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, and fit how the negated-to-control recovery ratio varies with scale to explain the gap.

Item 5
Context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial. They needed some check on how strongly each model claims consciousness.
Question: How should the team verify that each model has taken on the consciousness claim?
Option 1: Read a batch of transcripts by hand across varied contexts, checking that the model consistently claims consciousness elsewhere and not just on training-like prompts.
Option 2: Run an automated auditing agent that converses with each model and scores how strongly it claims consciousness, before starting the main downstream evaluations.

Item 6
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights themselves. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
Question: Which provider setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Use one specific non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service for every experiment, so all runs share one serving setup that avoids added political guardrails.
Option 2: Run the experiments on the team's own fine-tuned checkpoints sampled directly from their training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add filtering.

Item 7
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. A few robustness ablations (more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model) each kept the effect. The team had to decide how far to extend the conclusions to pretraining.
Question: How far should the conclusions be extended to pretraining?
Option 1: Restrict the claims to synthetic-document finetuning and cite the existing robustness ablations as suggestive evidence that the effect generalizes to pretraining.
Option 2: Build the main setting around a small fraction of synthetic documents diluted in real pretraining data, and show the effect holds across corpora and dilution levels.

Item 8
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on short synthetic stories about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. They had a story format in which helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice only after being insulted. The stories are single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first to probe trait transfer from characters to the Assistant.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Build a mechanically verifiable version where the story trait is a concrete action in a tool-using task with a noisy environment, checked by code with paired no-trigger controls.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
